17 A parachutist is falling towards the ground at a constant speed v. The rate at which she is losing
gravitational potential energy is R.
The acceleration of free fall is g.
What is the mass of the parachutist?

gv

hints: Notice the parachutist falls distance $v \times t$ in time $t$ at constant speed $v$, so focus on change in $mgh$ per unit time.
Recall that power or rate of energy transfer equals force times velocity for motion along the force, here weight $mg$ times $v$.
Set the given rate $R$ equal to $mgv$ and rearrange to make mass $m$ the subject before checking the options.
walkthrough: Identify what is given: constant downward speed $v$, rate of loss of gravitational potential energy $R$ in $\text{J s}^{-1}$, and $g$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
State the physics: in time $t$ she falls distance $h = vt$, so loss of potential energy is $\Delta E_p = mgh = mgvt$.
Rate of loss is energy divided by time: $R = \Delta E_p / t = mgvt / t = mgv$.
Rearrange for mass: divide both sides by $gv$ to get $m = R/(gv)$.
Check units: $R$ in watts divided by $gv$ in $\text{m}^2 \text{s}^{-3}$ gives $\text{kg}$, as required for mass. This is option B

A.explanation: This is $gv$ divided by $R$, which is the reciprocal of the correct relation and has units of $\text{kg}^{-1}$ not $\text{kg}$.

B.explanation: Rate of loss of $mgh$ equals $mgv$, so $R = mgv$ gives $m = R/(gv)$.

C.explanation: This uses $2R/v^2$, which comes from kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and ignores gravitational potential loss at rate $R$.

D.explanation: This is $v^2/(2R)$, which is inverted and based on kinetic energy, not on power $mgv$.
